hops.title: Why there is still room for dessert
hops.text: You are too full for another forkful of pasta, yet two minutes later a cookie looks fine. Barbara Rolls and colleagues tested this in 1984. Their study of 48 volunteers compared two four-course lunches: one served the same food four times, the other four different foods. With variety, people ate 60% more calories, mostly in the third and fourth courses. The rated pleasantness of each food fell quickly as it was eaten, while uneaten foods held up. Eating a savory food lowered the appeal of other savory foods more than sweet ones, and the reverse held for sweet. The food just eaten lost the most appeal.

sources.citation: Rolls BJ, Van Duijvenvoorde PM, Rolls ET (1984). Pleasantness changes and food intake in a varied four-course meal. Appetite 5(4):337-348.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A half-eaten plate of pasta pushed slightly back beside a small plate with a chocolate-chip cookie and sliced strawberries.
image.caption: Eating one food lowers its value, while a food of a different kind stays appealing.

hops.afterHeading: Hunger: a fuel gauge and two opposed groups of neurons
hops.title: Why some Labradors are so keen on food
hops.text: About 22% of UK pet Labrador retrievers carry a 14-base-pair deletion in the POMC gene. The deletion stops that copy of the gene from making two of its usual peptides, one of which activates MC4R, the stop button, much as alpha-MSH does. Each copy was linked to about 1.9 kilograms more body weight on average. Three hours after a standard meal, carriers spent longer investigating a perforated box with a sausage inside than noncarriers did. In one assistance-dog breeding program, about three quarters of 81 Labradors carried the deletion. The authors suggest that dogs keen on food may be easier to train with food rewards, though that is not proven.

sources.citation: Raffan E et al. (2016). A Deletion in the Canine POMC Gene Is Associated with Weight and Appetite in Obesity-Prone Labrador Retriever Dogs. Cell Metabolism 23(5):893-900.
Dittmann MT, Raffan E et al. (2024). Low resting metabolic rate and increased hunger due to beta-MSH and beta-endorphin deletion in a canine model. Science Advances 10(10):eadj3823.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A golden Labrador retriever in a plain harness staring closely at a sausage sealed inside a clear perforated plastic box.
image.caption: Labradors carrying a POMC deletion spent longer investigating a box with a sausage sealed inside.

hops.afterHeading: In addiction, wanting can grow while liking does not
hops.title: Three thousand lever presses for a dose without significantly higher liking ratings
hops.text: In 1991, researchers at the National Institute on Drug Abuse asked five volunteers with histories of heroin use to work for a weekday injection. The price was 3,000 lever presses: 30 rounds of 100, with a brief light after each round. Placebo did not keep anyone pressing. At the lowest morphine dose tested, four of the five kept responding. Yet on their questionnaires, grouped liking ratings at that dose showed no statistically significant increase over placebo. The drug kept their behavior going even though the group's reported liking did not rise significantly above placebo.

sources.citation: Lamb RJ, Preston KL, Schindler CW, Meisch RA, Davis F, Katz JL, Henningfield JE, Goldberg SR (1991). The reinforcing and subjective effects of morphine in post-addicts: a dose-response study. Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics 259(3):1165-1173.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage laboratory box with a single brass lever and a small glowing amber light on a wooden desk.
image.caption: Four of five volunteers kept pressing for low-dose morphine, while group liking ratings were not significantly above placebo.

audio.title: Cavefish, momentary happiness and rats that chase a lever
audio.transcript: Here are three more stories, one for each part of this lesson: a hunger circuit tuned by evolution, how surprising outcomes can shift happiness, and a food cue that some rats learn to approach. First, a fish. The Mexican tetra is a small river fish, and some of its populations colonized dark caves. Cavefish and surface fish are the same species. Dark caves can be nutrient-poor, with episodic inputs from outside such as floods and bats, while some cavefish populations feed in both wet and dry seasons on varying diets including detritus, plant material and aquatic invertebrates. In twenty fifteen, Aspiras and colleagues compared cave populations with their surface cousins. All the cave populations they tested lost weight more slowly than surface fish during a two-month fast, and some of them also ate more than surface fish when fed. When the team looked at appetite genes, they found coding mutations in M C four R, the same receptor this lesson calls a stop button. One of the changed sites matches a site linked to obesity in people. Tested in cells, the mutated cave version of the receptor had lower resting activity and a weaker maximal response. In laboratory crosses, three-month-old Pachón fish with two copies of the Tinaja cave version had higher food intake adjusted for body condition than one-copy fish. Fasted at nine months after a borderline body-length comparison, two-copy fish in that cohort lost a smaller percentage of weight, though tests in older fish found no significant appetite difference. The authors suggest this variant could offer a selective advantage in nutrient-poor caves. Second, how does a surprise change how happy you feel during a game? You might expect your mood to track how much money you have won so far. In twenty fourteen, Robb Rutledge and colleagues, including Peter Dayan, one of the scientists behind the temporal-difference model of dopamine, tested that idea. People played a chance-based reward task and rated their happiness again and again, first in the lab and then in a large replication with eighteen thousand four hundred twenty participants. Recent events explained momentary happiness better than total earnings did. Three recent ingredients mattered: chosen sure rewards, what people expected from chosen gambles, and the prediction errors on those gambles, where outcomes better than expected lifted mood and outcomes worse than expected lowered it. In functional M R I scans, activity in the striatum tracked those same expectations and prediction errors. In this task, recent sure rewards, gamble expectations and surprises explained the ratings better than the running total did. Third, a food cue that some rats learn to approach. Put a rat in a chamber where a metal lever slides in for a few seconds just before a food pellet drops into a separate tray. The rat never has to touch the lever; the pellet comes either way. Rats vary in where they go when the lever appears, and in twenty eleven Shelly Flagel and colleagues studied two contrasting patterns. Goal-trackers glance at the lever and go to the food tray. Sign-trackers go to the lever itself and engage with it, as if the signal were the reward. Both groups learned at the same rate. The team measured fast dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens as the rats learned. Only in sign-trackers did the dopamine response shift from the food to the lever. Then they gave flupenthixol, a drug that blocks dopamine receptors, during training, suppressing both responses while the drug was active. On a later drug-free test, goal-trackers went to the food tray when the lever appeared, while sign-trackers had not learned to approach the lever. In this experiment, blocking dopamine receptors during training stopped sign-tracking from developing, while goal-tracking developed anyway.
